1.point: Open with Abu Dharr, raise the orientalists' question of where the road came from, and announce the chapter's answer: the Qur'an, the Prophet and the Imams.
steps: Hook: Abu Dharr's lonely death and the question of what drove him
Widen the question to the whole road and state Mutahhari's two options (grown inside Islam vs imported)

2.point: The road's raw material was present in Islam's first generation: in the Qur'an, in the Prophet and his companions, and most fully in Imam Ali and the Imams after him.
steps: Set out the opposing three-part picture (distant God, fear-and-hope piety, merely pious companions)
Qur'an: God is near, and the Qur'an has the road's own vocabulary
Prophet: his piety is one of love and ecstasy, not fear and hope only
Companions: named mystics in the full sense
Imam Ali holds the teaching most fully; chains trace to him
The later Imams taught the same
Evidence in the supplications the reader already recites

3.point: The next generation of seekers learned from the Imams, directly or through Imam Ali's companions, and were plainly their inferiors.
steps: The line runs from Imam Ali's companions to the second-century seekers
The master of each type (fear, renunciation, love) learned from an Imam of his day
Explain why most famous names are nonetheless Sunni (danger under the Umayyads; the Imams' followers never spoke of themselves)
The seekers stood below the Imams: their teaching is an echo; the Shaqiq story shows the gap

4.point: The road was not imported; at most some techniques were borrowed, and only the later theory drew on outside ideas.
steps: State the three proposed outside sources and why Western writers sought them
Christian monks: the case rests on wool; the Qur'an disowns monasticism; celibacy and lodges differ
Neoplatonism: reached only the later theorists, not the early seekers
Buddhism: strongest case, but concepts differ and the attitude came from the Qur'an and Imam al-Sadiq; techniques at most

¶1.label: advance
¶1.why: The hook: Abu Dharr's outspokenness, exile and lonely death, which ¶2 turns into the orientalists' question.

¶2.label: advance
¶2.why: Raises the question (what motivated Abu Dharr, and by extension the whole road), states Mutahhari's two options and announces the chapter's answer.

¶3.label: advance
¶3.why: Sets up the three-part opposing picture that ¶4-¶7 dismantle in turn; the section's structure depends on it.

¶4.label: advance
¶4.why: First part answered: the Qur'an pictures God as everywhere and with everything, introducing the verse.

¶5.label: support
¶5.why: Reads the verse for the nearness claim and gives the Qur'an's own vocabulary for the road (liqa', states of the self, purification, love); evidence the Qur'an step rests on.

¶6.label: advance
¶6.why: Second part answered: the Prophet's own piety is one of spiritual love and ecstasy, not only fear and hope.

¶7.label: advance
¶7.why: Third part answered: the companions were mystics in the full sense, with the three names the sources agree on.

¶8.label: advance
¶8.why: New step: among the companions the teaching is held most fully by Imam Ali, with Tabataba'i's contrast and the chains traced to him.

¶9.label: advance
¶9.why: New step: the Imams after Ali taught the same, with Schimmel on Imam al-Sadiq.

¶10.label: support
¶10.why: Evidence for the Imams' teaching in the supplications the reader already recites; it grounds ¶9's claim in material the reader can check.

¶11.label: restate
¶11.why: Summarises the section's steps; the point is stated again in the words of the section heading.

¶12.label: advance
¶12.why: Establishes the line from Imam Ali's companions to the next generation (Tabataba'i's 'first group') and sets up the three masters to come.

¶13.label: advance
¶13.why: Fear: Fudayl and Lantern of the Path under Imam al-Sadiq's name; first of the three masters.

¶14.label: advance
¶14.why: Renunciation: Ibrahim ibn Adham learned from Imam al-Sadiq; his three levels traced to the Imams, introducing the Nahj al-Balagha quotation.

¶15.label: support
¶15.why: Explains the quotation and ties the third level to Imam Ali's saying, which ¶14's claim that the ideas trace to the Imams needs.

¶16.label: advance
¶16.why: Love: Ma'ruf al-Karkhi under Imam al-Rida; notes Rabi'a as the exception, which ¶20 uses.

¶17.label: advance
¶17.why: Raises the objection the chain must answer (most names are Sunni) and promises two reasons; ¶18-¶19 deliver them.

¶18.label: advance
¶18.why: First reason: naming the Imams was dangerous under the Umayyads, with Hasan al-Basri and Shaqiq as cases.

¶19.label: advance
¶19.why: Second reason: the Imams' followers never spoke of themselves, and Tabataba'i's finding that the early visions mostly match the Imams' sayings.

¶20.label: advance
¶20.why: Supplies the second half of the point: the seekers stood below the Imams (echo; Rabi'a against the Whispered Prayer; the definition of love is the Imams' own).

¶21.label: support
¶21.why: Opens the Shaqiq story, the extended example for ¶20's 'stood below' step; ¶25 draws on it.

¶22.label: support
¶22.why: First of the two answerings from the Qur'an that ¶25 cites; part of the example ¶20 needs.

¶23.label: support
¶23.why: Second answering, which ¶24 and ¶25 count ('twice'); still the example in motion. The story runs long for one step but each beat is used.

¶24.label: support
¶24.why: The reveal that the young man was Imam al-Kazim, which gives the story its force for ¶25; Mutahhari's corroboration is a minor extra.

¶25.label: restate
¶25.why: Draws a moral already stated in ¶20 ('without ever standing level') and already observed in ¶24 ('twice now'); the Sheikh's quote adds no new step.

¶26.label: restate
¶26.why: Repeats the section point in its heading's words.

¶27.label: advance
¶27.why: States why Western writers looked outside and names the three proposed sources the section will take in turn.

¶28.label: advance
¶28.why: Christian monks: states the case (wool) and introduces the Qur'an's own verdict on monasticism.

¶29.label: advance
¶29.why: Refutes the Christian case: a road grown from the Qur'an had no warrant to copy monasticism; celibacy and lodges differ.

¶30.label: advance
¶30.why: Neoplatonism: reached only the later theorists, and supplies the 'later theory drew on outside ideas' half of the point via Mutahhari's third view.

¶31.label: advance
¶31.why: Buddhism: the strongest case, answered by the difference in concepts, the Qur'anic attitude and Ibrahim's teacher; supplies 'techniques at most'.

¶32.label: restate
¶32.why: Mutahhari's verdict that the basic sources are Islam repeats what ¶27-¶31 have just shown and what ¶2 announced; the deferral to separate study adds no step.

¶33.label: aside
¶33.why: Nicholson, Massignon and Schimmel conceding the same conclusion: further scholars saying the same thing. Deleting it leaves no step unsupported.

¶34.label: restate
¶34.why: Jurdaq's pitcher-and-sea image restates the thesis and ¶32's verdict in a metaphor; it closes the Abu Dharr frame but adds no link.

¶35.label: restate
¶35.why: Chapter-level summary of all three sections' points.

¶36.label: aside
¶36.why: A question the chapter does not answer, left as a bridge to the next chapter; the argument does not use it.
